# gptr <picture><source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Broccolito/gptr/main/man/figures/logo-dark.png"/><img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Broccolito/gptr/main/man/figures/logo.png" align="right" width="120" height="139" alt="gptr logo"/></picture>

gptr runs language model agents inside your live R session, using **in-memory compute**.
They work with objects you already loaded and reuse your variables and intermediate results
across turns. With enough available memory, this includes datasets around **4 GB or larger**.
Load a dataset once, analyze it by name, and rerun the step you want to change. One function,
`peter()`, is an interactive chat in the console and a programmable call that you put in
scripts, loops and `if` statements.

The model receives bounded descriptions, previews and tool output; the R tool computes on the
full object in your session. See `vignette("execution-model", package = "gptr")` for memory and
data-sharing details.

- **One function.** `peter()` with no prompt opens a chat at the console; with a prompt it runs
  the agent and returns the session, which the pipe steers:
  `peter("...") |> peter("...")`.
- **System 1 and System 2.** Conversational models (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini,
  OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Ollama, and the Claude Code and Codex CLIs) run agents; typed
  decision models such as TypeSafe AI's Jev and Clef return yes/no, choice and score answers
  that go straight into `if` and `for`.
- **The script is the history.** gptr can record executed agent code into your `.R`, `.Rmd`,
  `.qmd` or `.ipynb` document. Fresh recorded blocks replay without model calls; supply their
  required input data and packages when replaying in a fresh session.
- **Everything is R.** Tools are R functions; artifacts are Shiny apps; skills, MCP servers,
  sub-agents, hooks and plugins use one documented extension API.
- **Safe defaults.** The default `manual` mode runs read-only actions and asks before changes.
  The permission gate is not a sandbox; see `?gptr_security`.

Read the [guides and function reference](https://broccolito.github.io/gptr/) online.

## Installation

Install gptr from CRAN, or the development version from GitHub, with R 4.2 or later:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("gptr")
pak::pak("Broccolito/gptr")
```

This README documents gptr 1.0; the 0.7 API is different, so check that `packageVersion("gptr")`
is at least 1.0.0. No model server or CLI is required for the offline examples below.

## Connect a model

For an interactive first session, sign in to the Claude Code CLI or the Codex CLI outside R,
then call `peter()`; with no default model it offers to save one. See
`vignette("interactive-console", package = "gptr")`.

Choose a provider explicitly before your first real call. API credentials and CLI sign-in are
separate routes; see `vignette("language-models")`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gptr_env("~/keys/.env")          # provider keys, e.g. OPENAI_API_KEY
gptr_providers()                 # what is configured
gptr_config(model = "openai/gpt-6-sol", .scope = "session")
peter()                          # chat in the console
```

In the chat you can keep typing while Peter works: in a terminal, Enter steers the running answer
and Tab queues a follow-up for the next prompt. `/help` lists the commands and keys.

## A first session

With a configured model, tell Peter what to do:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(gptr)
session = peter("Fit mpg from wt in mtcars. Save the model as fit.", mtcars)
session |> peter("Plot fit's residuals and explain what they show.")
```

The pipe continues the same session. The usual permission checks apply.

<details>
<summary>Run this pattern offline</summary>

This scripted model needs no key or server. It supplies the tool code rather than generating it.

```{r}
library(gptr)

fake = gptr_fake_provider(list(
  list(tool = "r", input = list(code = "fit = lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)\ncoef(fit)")),
  "Each 1000 lb of weight lowers mpg by about 5.3.",
  list(tool = "r", input = list(code = "predicted = predict(fit)\nhead(predicted)")),
  "The predictions are stored in predicted."
))
work = new.env()
session = peter("Fit mpg from wt in mtcars. Save the model as fit.", mtcars,
  model = fake, envir = work, mode = auto)
session$text
ls(work)

session |> peter("Reuse fit to predict mpg for the same cars.")
head(work$predicted)
session$turns
```

The second turn reuses `fit`.

</details>

The same pattern works with a large object already in your workspace. This recipe does not
allocate or load a 4 GB dataset:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# counts is a numeric matrix, around 4 GB, already loaded in this R session.
session = peter(
  "Compute colSums(counts) as totals and return the six largest totals.",
  counts
)
session |> peter("Reuse totals to plot their distribution.")
```

A System 1 question returns a typed R vector with the probabilities attached:

<details>
<summary>Offline typed-decision example</summary>

```{r}
judge = gptr_fake_provider(list(0.93, 0.08), name = "judge", type = "classifier")
abstracts = c(a = "We randomized 200 adults to drug or placebo.",
              b = "We followed a cohort of nurses for 20 years.")
is_rct = peter("Is this abstract about a randomized controlled trial?", abstracts,
  model = judge)
as.logical(is_rct)
gptr_prob(is_rct)
```

</details>

## Local models with Ollama

Installed Ollama chat models run agents, for example `model = "ollama/qwen3:1.7b"`. Clef and
Clef Flash (Ollama 0.35.1 or later) return typed decisions, for example
`model = "ollama/clef-flash"`. gptr never installs Ollama or downloads models, and by default
never falls back to a cloud model; a workflow stays local only if every model and tool it uses
is local.

## Exporting recorded R

A synchronized `.R` history can become an ordinary R script or a script of `peter()` calls:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gptr_doc("analysis.R", sync = TRUE)
gptr_export("analysis.R", "analysis-raw.R")
gptr_export("analysis.R", "analysis-peter.R", format = "peter")
```

The default keeps recorded R executable and turns `peter()` calls into comments. The
`format = "peter"` output keeps calls active and recorded code inert, with bounded output and
notes beside the turns. Both preserve ordinary source and refuse stale or ambiguous records.
Export does not run or verify the result, recover unrecorded console work, or save your input
objects. See `vignette("script-as-history", package = "gptr")` for interleaved R and a second
session.

## Why Peter?

The package is `gptr`; you talk to its agent through `peter()`. The name honors two Peters:

- **Peter Naur**, the Danish computer scientist who edited the ALGOL 60 report and helped
  develop the syntax notation now called Backus-Naur Form. His work connects to gptr's
  readable R code and history documents.
- **Peter Cathcart Wason**, the cognitive psychologist who, with Jonathan Evans, studied
  dual processes in reasoning and the difference between a response and its conscious
  justification. His work connects to inspecting results, evidence and explanations.

gptr calls typed decision models "System 1" and conversational agents "System 2". These are
software roles; they do not imply human cognition or that Wason introduced those labels.
The `vignette("why-peter", package = "gptr")` guide gives the history and primary sources.

## Upgrading from gptr 0.7.0

gptr 1.0.0 is a complete rewrite. `get_response()` and `dataframe_to_text()` were removed:
use `peter("your prompt")$text` instead of `get_response()`, and pass a data frame to `peter()`
as context instead of converting it to text. See `NEWS.md`.

## Acknowledgments

gptr was inspired by Mario Zechner's 'pi' coding agent; its tool descriptions, edit semantics
and prompt-template grammar are derived from 'pi' (MIT license). The model catalog is derived from models.dev (MIT license) and the
secret patterns from gitleaks (MIT license), and the System 1 emulation prompt follows TypeSafe AI's
system-one-adapter-python (MIT license); see `inst/COPYRIGHTS`. Ideas were borrowed from
'ellmer', 'tidyllm', 'btw' and 'mcptools', none of which gptr depends on. Anthropic, OpenAI,
Google, TypeSafe AI, Ollama and the vendors of the command-line tools are third-party services;
